city-digital-twin · Newcastle study · project report

Project report #12 - the city digital twin, 16 September 2026

2026-09-16HEAD d6f9cdfbranch praneetdhoolia/eleventh-report-scoring-pairgate PASS

Built, measured three times, and the first controlled reading is a null. The twin runs all twelve modes in the mobsim on the real network and timetables, at 25 %, to a declared 250-iteration horizon, twice in one family (F35) without a stall, a gate or a heap event - 27.39 h for the routers pair. On the newest result 2 of 12 modes are inside 10 % (car, motorbike) and 6 are past the 20 % bar (ride, taxi, bike, heavy_rail, light_rail, ferry); ride's target sits above its choice-set coverage and no constant can reach it. The routers pair - the first recommended model-side control ever executed - moved nothing outside one build's noise, so router-scorer consistency is exonerated and the scoring pair (at_innovation_cutoff, the one field predicting the cutoff snap on both results) launched today on the committed build's own probe price. The code is disciplined where it matters (every value in the registry at 0 hardcoding; every check named for the incident it answers; nothing presents a non-result as a result) and heavy where it grew fast: two 500-800-line build functions, an events file parsed by three parsers, 60 of 189 Python modules and all of the Java untested. Two defects found this pass were fixed in the same tree before the report was written - the pricer's 22.8 h of phantom setup on an orphaned run, and every reader resolving residents through the city's current population (#213), which the roots rebuild scheduled beside the scoring pair would have tripped. The field survey's top rung is still empty across 55 agent-based city twins: this project remains the only one scoring every simulated mode against its own official figure with a band, and the only one with a controlled one-field fidelity reading. Twelve reports have not moved a mode across the 10 % line; what has (0 -> 2) was a network rebuild and the engines' routing. The open set is now the set of things that cost an approval, an external party or a family boundary - the scoring pair (running), the roots rebuild (next, re-scoped: the short-trip supply is already at the seed), the TfNSW request (the user's), the replication band.

Method

Read at HEAD d6f9cdf on branch praneetdhoolia/eleventh-report-scoring-pair, 16 September 2026, with in-flight work in the tree (described in its own section). Phase 1 ran the three collectors (metrics.json, code_metrics.json, performance.json; 322 dated events, 189 Python files / 61,219 lines, 60 Java files / 17,746 lines, 194 run directories). Phases 2-7 ran as six independent agents in parallel, one per phase, each writing its JSON before returning: a code reviewer over the six areas (thresholds from collect_code_metrics.py:47-58: LONG_FUNCTION 150, COMPLEX_FUNCTION 15, DEEP_NESTING 5, DUP_WINDOW 6 lines / 120 chars), a performance analyst over every run's own stopwatch, a historian over all 79 PRs and the 142 record rows, a document reviewer over every living and archived document, hook, workflow and skill, a field researcher (37 of 40 calls over 12 rounds, stopped by the two-barren-rounds rule) and a factor researcher (20 of 40 calls over 6 rounds). The rating rubric: five dimensions per area, 1-5, each cell with its two strongest pieces of evidence; a defect in the area caps correctness at 3; a 5 needs zero defects and no open risk; ratings are never averaged across areas. Depth of read was declared per area and is a blind spot of this pass, not a claim: build layer 12 of 39 files (~950 of 18,202 lines; write_day and the chains main unread line by line); run harness 14 of 16 (~5,700 of 7,211); analysis 9 of 41 (~900 of 16,252; 25 measure/diagnose modules unread); contract 9 of 71 plus a script over the 558 fields; acquisition 0 of 18 adapters whole (by grep, hosts sampled 12 of 12 allowed); MATSim extensions 8 of 60 (~1,400 of 17,746; the controler's assemble, the signal controllers and 18 config groups unread). The writer's own measurements: the sub-1 km supply at the seed (17.70 % of 2,225,609 core legs at <= 0.748 km straight-line), the pricer's setup on the orphaned pair, the reports index against the record. A 25 % pricing probe (20260916T053153_4it_25pct) ran on the machine throughout; no lane competed with it.

The timeline from day 0

  • 10 Aug: one day builds P0-P3 (three PRs, the package, the network, the demand) and P4 opens the next morning by discovering that none of the 30 run-input sets loads.
  • 11-16 Aug: one five-day PR (#38, 73 commits) declares every value in a registry, splits the city from the framework, and rebuilds the network because a typed harvest box had stranded 87 SA1s.
  • 16-24 Aug: the pilots and the calibrated base - two 1000-iteration arms at 25 % (F4, 67 h each) give C5; ride pairing is built and measured starved; every person mode becomes physical in a stack of six PRs that strands on its own base branches.
  • 24-25 Aug: the goal directive; SUMO descoped; the all-modes batch built inert then activated as F6; the documents pinned to artefacts; the first gate fires.
  • 26 Aug-1 Sep: the gate loop at full speed - F7 to F23 in seven days, eight families on 30 Aug alone, the demand rebuilt three times that day, twelve individual targets, the fare, the results store; the first mode inside 10 % at a gate (bus, 1 Sep).
  • 3-6 Sep: requirement 10 and the issue gate; the first project report and its 26 issues closed without a run; destinations balanced; a stopped run becomes citable; F24-F27.
  • 7-8 Sep: four reports in one day; car inside at the F28 gate; the holdout found informing the count targets; the iteration cut 310 -> 205 s and the 2-minute target priced out; the objective restated as the twelve-mode maximum; the search can run for the first time.
  • 9 Sep: the first RESULT since 21 Aug (F32, 21.5 h): 0 of 12 inside and relaxing made the fit worse - the car snap at the innovation cutoff.
  • 10-11 Sep: the choice-set ceiling (ride unreachable by any constant); the counts rung found on the wrong roads for 25 days; F33 rebuilt and its arm dead on a heap nobody set; the launcher taught to refuse it.
  • 12-14 Sep: the footpath network (F34), the engines route what they re-mode (F35), arm 0 runs 30 h to the second RESULT: 2 of 12 (car, motorbike) - from the rebuild and the routing, not from any recommended control.
  • 14 Sep: six PRs in one day - the documents move twice, the lane and the recommendations become ledgers, the run viewer is built three times over; the routers pair is launched at midnight.
  • 15-16 Sep: the pair runs to its horizon with its harness dead from iteration 34; closed out by a new sanctioned path as the third RESULT; it moves nothing. Twelve reports, 53 sessions, 35 families, 490 machine hours, 2 of 12.

Three questions

a_framework_tuned_to_newcastle
Mostly no, with four residues. (1) src/city.py:46 DEFAULT_CITY = 'newcastle' is the documented selector default (CLAUDE.md), a sanctioned literal. (2) config/schema/overlay.schema.json:34 closes day_type to WEEKDAY/SAT/SUN - one city's vocabulary in the portable half, unread by any consumer (F18, still open). (3) tests/check_city_agnostic.py:51 ALL_MODE_NAMES is a typed twelve-mode list and code_metrics literal_mode_lists names src/build/build_gtfs_extras.py:43 (bus/ferry/heavy_rail), build_matsim_run_inputs.py:436 (motorbike/ride/taxi/truck) and :1126 (bus/rail/tram), src/calibrate/measure_mode_constraints.py:51 (bike/pt/walk), report_mode_ridership.py:79/:458 and report_choice_set_coverage.py:76 - seven mode lists a metro/ferry-less city would have to edit. (4) src/build/build_matsim_network.py:94 JAVA_XMX = '-Xmx6g' and --workers 2 are this machine's values in the framework. No coordinate, extent, place name or CRS is typed in src/ (grep for -32./151./Newcastle/28356 over src: none outside docstrings); extents come from city.extent() and the LGA boundary, the CRS from city.crs(), the target LGA from city.target_lga(), the day types and base scenario from city.json (run.py:164-169). The default overlay run.py selects (default_25pct: 1000 iterations, 40g) is a city file but the framework names it (run.py:52).
b_non_result_presented_as_result
No path presents a stopped or failed run as a RESULT: every consumer that can say "result" gates on completion == ran_to_last_iteration (build_status_board.py:197, build_run_index.py:119, build_fit_figures.py:183-209, calibrate.py:459-465, run_view.py:535 with the horizon floor from the registry, find_completed run_matsim.py:1077). Two paths can present a reading on the WRONG BASIS: (1) build_status_board.py:174-183 reads a stopped arm at its newest trips table, which can be one iteration past _run.json reached_iteration when a kill lands between the trips write and the ENDS marker (risk, area 3); (2) extract_metrics.py:163 home_lga and (for a stopped arm) schedule_path :295-330 resolve through the CITY's current B1 and schedule, so a reading taken after a rebuild is on a different resident set - live under the D7 note that the roots rebuild proceeds in parallel with the scoring pair. One path UNDERSTATES a reading: run_matsim.py:1817 close_out via --stop on an orphan records reached_iteration from the harness's digest, not the log (defect, area 2). The in-flight work presents nothing as a result; lane.json D5/D6/D7 answers are decisions, and the routers pair's record (ran_to_last_iteration, 250, closed_out_by run.py --close-out) was read from disk.
c_which_check_catches_each_defect
area 1 defect - build_population.py:332/:358 household_size_top_band_mean unreachable
none today. check_hardcoding.key_uses counts the key as wired by its string at :39; no unit test imports build_population; the sweep ledger would show a zero sensitivity only after a sweep arm. Guard to write: a unit test on a one-SA1 fixture asserting the mean drawn household size moves with the field, or a key_uses extension that requires a declared artefact column per build-stage field.
area 2 defect - run_matsim.py:1817 (+ :465-475) orphan stopped by --stop recorded at the digest's iteration
none today. tests/unit/test_close_out_orphan.py covers --close-out at the horizon (which bypasses the digest) and test_stop_run.py covers a stop with a live harness whose digest is complete; neither builds a memo shorter than the log. Guard to write: a unit test with _progress.json to 34 and a matsim.log with ENDS markers to 180, asserting stop_run's record says 180.

Two layers with one resolver between them: src/build/ is the framework (population, chains, plans, network, run-input assembly, manifest) and cities/newcastle/build/ is the city (targets, corridor, signals, crossings, schedules). Every script imports registry at module import and reads its constants into ALL-CAPS module globals (build_activity_chains.py:62-401 is 60 such reads), then main() streams CSVs and writes artefacts under city.path(). Determinism is by seeded numpy Generators (build_population.py:279, build_activity_chains.py:1807/2305/2867, build_matsim_plans.py:1418/1422) and blake2b unit hashes shared with the sampler; wall-clock appears only in provenance stamps and build_timing. The assembler (build_matsim_run_inputs.py) is also imported by the run harness so the shipped config and the run config are emitted by one path. The weakness is shape, not correctness: the three largest scripts carry 846-, 510- and 383-line functions, the network is decoded six times per scenario, and the B2/B1 CSVs are streamed three times per plans build.

architecture
run.py parses, runs the issue gate once, resolves the registry, runs preflight() (every refusal but the subsample, into a temp dir), and - in the in-flight D6 change - registers a Task Scheduler one-shot that re-invokes itself with --issue-gate-passed --foreground unless --foreground or --dry-run was given; CITYSIM_LAUNCH_STAMP makes the task and the run directory share one stamp so --stop can find both. run_matsim.run() names the directory, writes the status card, emits the config through the same registry emitter the builder uses, launches the JVM with stdout redirected to matsim.log, and starts three daemon watchers (gate every N iterations via the reporter subprocess, ceiling on wall clock, stall on log mtime), each writing a marker file BEFORE proc.kill() so whichever process reaches the terminal record finds the cause. close_out() writes _run.json with completion in {ran_to_last_iteration, stopped_at_gate/ceiling/stall, stopped_by_operator}; a crash gets no record. results_store owns every path under results/ and trims raw oldest-first once processed holds the findings. The two things that reach beyond one process - a harness that dies under a live JVM (orphan) and a second harness starting while one runs - are handled by reconcile_stale(), close_out_orphan() and procs.arm_running(), and those are where the seams show.

defectsrc/run/run_matsim.py1,840close_out() takes reached_iteration = max(per) (:1840) where per = iteration_times(log) (:507-516), which PREFERS the digest's _progress.json iteration_seconds and falls back to the log only when the digest is empty. For an ORPHAN - a harness dead at iteration k while the JVM runs on, the 9.176 shape - the digest stops at k, so stop_run (:1953-1954, which passes no reached_iteration) records reached_iteration = k and median_iteration_s over k iterations; reconcile_stale (:1240 via _last_completed_iteration :1358-1378) reads the same digest first. Only close_out_orphan (:2035 _iteration_times_from_log, :2058 reached_iteration=horizon) avoids it, and its own docstring says why the digest must not be trusted. watch_run.py:273-275 and run_failure.py:357-362 tell the operator to run.py --stop an orphan mid-run, which is exactly the path that understates it.Harness dies at iteration 34 (memo holds 0..34); the JVM reaches 180; the operator runs run.py --stop <run> --cause ... as the ORPHANED line instructs. _run.json says reached_iteration 34, completion stopped_by_operator; extract_metrics reads ITERS/it.30 as the arm's reading; the board says the run is citable at 34 and nowhere past it; the 146 iterations that were executed and whose trips tables sit on disk are never a reading, and the record's median is over 34 iterations.nonew

architecture
Three tiers over the run directory. Readers (extract_metrics, iteration_trips, iteration_reading, measure_iteration_modes) turn MATSim tables into rows, memoised per process; the reporter (report_mode_ridership) composes the twelve-mode reading from them and is invoked as a SUBPROCESS by the gate watcher, the store's extract, the viewer (since #225) and watch_run, writing a per-iteration memo under _trend/; the fit (calibrate/fit.py) scores only calibration rows and lists the unscorable; the board, the run index, the fit figures and the calibrator each re-read _run.json and gate on completion == ran_to_last_iteration (build_status_board.py:197, build_run_index.py:119, build_fit_figures.py:183-209, calibrate.py:459-465). The joins that decide who is a resident (home_lga) and which stop a boarding was at (schedule_path) resolve through the CITY's current artefacts when the run has no output copy, which is the seam a parallel rebuild opens. The viewer is a ThreadingMixIn HTTP server whose caches are now bounded and locked and whose readings come from a subprocess, closing the tenth report's two defects.

architecture
The contract is the registry schema plus a resolver that every script calls at import (load(strict=True) re-reads and re-validates 558 fields per process); the checks are three rings. Ring one is intrinsic (registry/__init__.py:229-300): required keys, sweep/held/derived presence, numeric leaves inside interval sweeps, derived_from integrity. Ring two is textual: check_hardcoding scans source for keys-as-strings (wired), template literals, inline numerics and coordinates against a hand-kept STRUCTURAL allowlist; check_city and check_city_agnostic prove a fixture city resolves and emits. Ring three is the document set: currency, shape, links, board blocks, lane ledger. CI runs rings one to three without data (nothing downloads, nothing runs); the unit job installs pandas only, so any test that imports geopandas skips. What no ring can see: whether a build-stage field MOVES an artefact (key_uses proves presence), a categorical sweep's membership for the declared value, a dict-valued field against a categorical sweep, an ALL-CAPS assignment whose value is an expression, and anything under tests/check_package.py, which is local only.

architecture
Fetch adapters download into data/raw with a provenance JSON (URL, sha256, retrieved date from the wall clock or the file mtime when re-run), and extract adapters turn raw into processed CSVs under city.path(); the manifest builder hashes everything, resolves lineage from each script's OUTPUT_INPUTS declaration and stamps licence and share-alike verdicts. Extents are derived (overpass.py:61-97 from the LGA boundary and A.osm.*_margin_m) rather than typed; hosts are all inside the sandbox allowlist. The validation targets are split by row label (calibration/holdout) with the count stations split on the published permanent_station flag, and the holdout is enforced by each reader filtering on that label - no file-level separation exists.

architecture
CitysimControler.assemble() registers 19 ConfigGroups and binds every extension into one Controler: scoring handlers (fare, parking, crowding, service quality, bike stress) collect events into per-handler maps and emit money/score terms at AfterMobsim; qsim engines (JointRideEngine, GenericRouteTeleporter, HouseholdCarDepartureHandler, TaxiFleetEngine) claim departures on the qsim thread; RidePairingEngine runs at BeforeMobsim on stable plans, swaps its realised-time buffers there (deliberately not in reset), and routes detours on a per-iteration pool; EscortCoherenceListener proposes at Replanning with a Random seeded on (globalSeed + 7919 x iteration). Thread safety rests on two facts the harness enforces: one handler runs on one events thread, and RUN.machine.events_synchronize_on_simsteps publishes handler writes to the qsim thread (refuse_unsafe_telemetry); the signals stack alone uses ConcurrentHashMap/volatile explicitly. No leg is teleported silently: GenericRouteTeleporter throws on any declared network mode without a network route and counts every stub per mode; the one zero-time completion path (JointRideEngine wait timeout with an undefined route time) is the residual.

testability
No JUnit exists; the nine *Probe mains are the only executable specs and they print through System.out (42 sites). Python tests pin a few emitted strings (test_direct_walk_counters, test_raptor_mode_cost, test_pt_submode_choice, test_service_quality, test_plan_removal_one_selector) by reading the Java source as text, which proves a line exists, not that it runs. The engines take injected interfaces (EventsManager, InternalInterface, QNetsimEngineI) and would test on a two-link, two-agent qsim in seconds; the blocker is the toolchain (javac under .tools, no test runner in the pinned stack).

how_they_moved_F33_to_F35
At 25 % the plain iteration went 244.5 s (F33, road graph) → 555.5 s (F34, the footpath network: 181,892 → 368,230 links and every walk and pt access/egress leg executed on it) → 460.0 s (F35 probe: PersonPrepareForSim's whole-plan re-route removed, 92 → 2 s; the refused taxi walks now routed by the engine, 58–61 s at 81 % refusal) → 349 s on arm 0 and 346–368 s on the pair as the refusal count fell 45,573 → 2,214 and the router warmed. Against F32's 245 s plain iteration the F35 plain iteration is +42 %: mobsim 187 → 235–242 s (+26 % for 4.4× the departures, 623 k → 2.80 M), replanning 25 → 87–95 s (3.6×, the routers on the 368 k-link graph), prepareForMobsim 26 → 2 s, our listeners 4 → 16–20 s. The mobsim share fell 0.775 → 0.656 because replanning grew, not because the mobsim shrank.
share_of_this_project_own_java_on_the_newest_result
beforeMobsimListeners 16–20 s on a plain innovating iteration = RidePairingEngine.notifyBeforeMobsim 10–18 s (ride_pairing.csv elapsed_ms: 7,383 at it.0, 10,561 at it.98, 15,972 at it.198, 17,879 at it.249 — rising with the run) + TaxiFleetEngine's refused-walk routing 1.8–6.8 s (matsim.log 'taxiFleet: N refused trip(s) routed ... in M ms': 45,297 ms at it.0, 6,765 at it.99, 1,827 at it.250); iterationStarts / afterMobsim / scoring 0 s at whole-second resolution; iterationEnds 1–2 s plain (RunTelemetry's line + whole-day link file), 21–25 s on trips-table iterations, 46–86 s on plans milestones. Our own code is ~5 % of a plain iteration (§9.170 said 4–5 %).

mobsim

threads_vs_cores
RUN.machine.threads = 16 qsim threads, RUN.machine.replanning_threads = 20, RUN.machine.event_handler_threads = 4, on a 24-CPU host (gc.log 'CPUs: 24 total', performance.json host_cpu_count 24; 64,980 MB RAM). §9.147 probed the qsim thread count on the F27 stack: a plain iteration 270–272 s at 10, 267 at 16, 264–265 at 24 — the mobsim does not scale with qsim threads past 10; §9.59: 12 event-handler threads bought nothing, synchronizeOnSimSteps=false was a 65 s/iteration regression, oneThreadPerHandler is fatal on the pinned build.
qsim_settings_in_force
start 0 h, end 30 h, PassingQ link dynamics (~42 s/it over FIFO at the §9.59 event volume, kept on correctness), traffic dynamics queue, stuck time 10 s, remove_stuck_vehicles false, vehicle_behavior teleport, vehicles from modeVehicleTypesFromVehiclesData, main modes car/truck/motorbike/walk/bike/taxi (walk and bike are physical on the network), snapshots off, flow/storage capacity factors derived from the 0.25 fraction (storage exponent 1.0), transit capacity scaled with floor 1.
pt_vehicles
2,139 transit vehicles of 4 types (output_transitVehicles.xml.gz of the pair); 391,684 vehicles in all (output_allVehicles.xml.gz: the roster's household cars, bikes, walkers' pce-0 vehicles, trucks, taxis).
departures_and_stuck
the pair's telemetry.jsonl at it.250: 2,837,001 departures — car 390,541, walk 1,115,560, non_network_walk 1,189,319 (the access/egress stage legs of every network trip), ride 64,846, bike 28,462, truck 23,891, bus 9,710, taxi 9,551, rail 3,262, motorbike 1,348, ferry 291, tram 220; stuck 2,317 (walk 1,697, bus 265, car 135); median over the run 2,797,111 departures and 4,515 stuck (0.16 %); early iterations ~21,300 stuck (the 4-iteration probes). 2.3 M of the 2.84 M departures are walk-type legs the qsim executes on the network since F34 — on F33's road graph the same population produced 634,899 departures (walk 209,559, no non_network_walk row).
departures_per_wall_second
collect_performance divides an iteration's total departures by RunTelemetry's iteration wall (wall_s = iterationStartedMs → iteration end, not the mobsim alone): pair median 7,610.9/s, arm 0 8,058.5/s, F33 probe 2,387.6/s, F32 result 2,555.2/s, 1 % F35 probe 1,922/s. Over the mobsim phase alone the pair moves ~11,500 departures per wall second (2.8 M / 242 s).
mobsim_cost_on_the_newest_result
233–245 s on a plain innovating iteration (66 % of 368 s; 64 % of the undisturbed 346.5 s), 252 s in the tail (86 % of 285 s); +230 s when the events file is written inside it (it.100 472 s, it.200 479 s) and +160 s at the last iteration (405 s). From the F34 JFR probe (§9.168, 20260912T162831): the mobsim was 24 % of CPU samples and the events pipeline 13.6 % for 57 % of the wall — the phase runs at low parallel efficiency, consistent with the flat thread scaling of §9.147. What serialises it (the 4-thread events pipeline under the simstep barrier, TransitQSimEngine, the signals controllers, the departure handlers) is unmeasured — needs a probe arm with JFR thread-state sampling (RUN.machine.jfr_profile true; src/analyse/profile_run.py exists).
scaling_with_fraction
sampling-and-families.md states no scaling law: it says the threshold between 10 % and 25 % is unmeasured (§9.12) and refuses cross-fraction comparison. Measured on F35's own probes: 1 % (20260912T184134) 50.4 s median with the mobsim ~35 s; 25 % (the pair) 346–368 s with the mobsim 233–245 s — 25× the households cost 7× in the mobsim, 10–15× in replanning (9 → 87–133 s), 7–9× overall. Per departure the 25 % mobsim is cheaper (96,562 departures in ~35 s = 2,760/s at 1 % against ~11,500/s at 25 %): the fixed per-iteration cost (transit fleet at full timetable, the 368 k-link graph, the barrier) dominates at 1 %. No 10 % run since F23 carries a stopwatch, so the 10 %/25 % relation is unmeasured on any current stack.
pace_band
RUN.monitor.pace_band_s = [217, 253] (registry, 'measured' on the F4-era 25 % × 1000 arm) flagged every iteration of both F35 results out of band (_progress.json pace.median_in_band false, solo_in_band false at 443–478 s); the position page already says the flag means nothing until re-measured. The pair's own band: 330–370 s innovating undisturbed, 262–320 s tail.

replanning

strategy_weights
RUN.replanning.weights ChangeExpBeta 0.7, ReRoute 0.15, SubtourModeChoice 0.1 (person subpopulation only), TimeAllocationMutator 0.05 (range 1800 s); subpopulations person/external/freight; plan memory RUN.replanning.max_agent_plan_memory = 8 (WorstPlanSelector for removal); brain_exp_beta 1.0; routing_randomness 3.0; access/egress accessEgressModeToLink with consistency check 'reroute'.
innovation_off
RUN.replanning.fraction_to_disable_innovation 0.8: cutoff at 200 of 250 on the pair (arm 0: 240 of 300); score MSA absent on both results (the in-flight scoring pair turns it on at the cutoff).
router_calls_per_iteration
not counted by any artefact. What the stopwatch and the log separate: MATSim's replanning phase 84–95 s on an undisturbed innovating iteration (ReRoute 15 % + SubtourModeChoice 10 % of 155,233 persons re-routed through PlanRouter on the 368 k-link graph; SpeedyALT.calcLeastCostPathImpl 34.5 % of CPU samples, NetworkDirectWalkPtRouter.calcRoute 16.0 % with 203,447 of 300,000 pt requests finding no transit route, §9.168, #162 awaiting-run), plus this project's own router use outside that phase: 2,214–47,783 refused taxi walks (1.8–58 s) and 588–644 unpaired ride legs (0.6–0.9 s) in beforeMobsimListeners, and the carrying drivers' detours inside the pairing pass. PersonPrepareForSim's per-iteration re-route is gone (26 → 2 s).
tail_vs_innovating_on_the_pair
innovating plain median 368 s (346.5 s undisturbed, it.100–180) against the post-cutoff tail's 285 s (262–320 s undisturbed): the cutoff removes 85–93 s of replanning (95 → 2 s) and nothing else — the mobsim is 242 → 252 s, our listeners 20 → 18 s (ride pairing keeps running: 13.7–17.9 s at it.249–250). The 44 plain tail iterations cost 13,367 s (13.8 % of the run) at 0.020 replanning share; arm 0's 53-iteration tail 262 s median at 0.009. F32's tail was 232.5 against 245 innovating (replanning was only 25 s there).
what_the_cutoff_split_prices
for a 250-iteration arm on the pair's clock: 175 × 368 + 44 × 285 + milestones 4,406 + it.0/1 1,352 + last 721 + setup/shutdown 1,868 = 98,590 s = 27.39 h, which is the landing; the 422 s single-median quote gave 30.0 h (+9.5 %), arm_cost's one-median idiom on arm 0 had given 39.0 h against 30.35 h (−22 %). Moving the cutoff 0.8 → 0.9 would ADD 25 × (368 − 285) ≈ 35 min per arm and opens a family (it is the search).

writing

intervals_in_force
RUN.controler.write_trips_interval 10 (registry), write_events_interval 100 (registry), write_plans_interval 25 on every F35 arm overlay (registry 100; the overlays set 25 for a warm start within 25 iterations, #192; the in-flight f35_scoring_msa_25pct keeps 25), create_graphs false, compression gzip, linkstats on MATSim's default cadence (5 files on the pair: it.100/150/200/250 + the average window).
which_iterations_dump_what_on_the_pair
plans.xml.gz at it.0, 1, 25, 50 … 250 (12 dumps, 10.85 GB, 0.90 GB each); experienced_plans.xml.gz + experienced_plans_scores at the same 11 milestones after it.1 (3.12 GB + 86 MB); events.xml.gz at it.0, 100, 200, 250 (4 files, 6.10 GB, 1.52 GB each) with signalEvents2Via.csv beside each (144 MB); trips/legs/activities.csv.gz every 10 (27 each: 0.49 + 1.26 + 0.33 GB); linkstats.txt.gz 5 × 30 MB; legHistogram/legdurations every iteration (17 MB in all); the final output_* set (events 1.56 GB, plans 0.91 GB, experienced 0.29 GB). Run directory 25.5 GB (arm 0 28.4 GB; the F32 result 11.3 GB with plans every 100).
what_each_dump_costs_in_wall
from the pair's stopwatch: a plans dump 185–230 s ('dump all plans', median 197 s, inside beforeMobsimListeners, 11 dumps 2,261 s = 2.3 % of the run — 'dump all plans share'); the experienced plans + scores + linkstats at the same milestone +46–86 s in iterationEndsListeners; the trips/legs/activities tables +20–25 s in iterationEndsListeners every 10th iteration (20 × ~21 s = 7 min); the events file +230 s inside the mobsim at it.100/200 and +160 s at it.250; it.0 and it.1 pay 757 and 595 s (the first dump, the first events file, cold routers). All milestone excess over the plain/tail base: 4,406 s = 1.22 h = 4.6 % of the pair (arm 0: 5,014 s = 1.39 h, 4.7 %; F32 with plans every 100: 1,468 s = 1.9 %).
bulk_vs_store_budget
results/raw is capped at RUN.storage.raw_cap_gb 500 GiB (536.9 GB), trimmed oldest-first, never a live run, never a run whose findings are not in processed/. On disk today (performance.json bytes_on_disk): 253.0 GB in all — completed 147.7 GB, aborted 102.0 GB, failed 3.3 GB, running 0.02 GB — 47 % of the cap; a 250-iteration arm at plans-every-25 adds ~25 GB, so ~11 more arms fit before the trim starts deleting the oldest reconstructible runs.
observers_per_cycle
progress digest (src/analyse/progress_digest.py, RUN.monitor.progress_interval_s 30 s): run_view.scan() — the log read incrementally from the last offset (run_view.py:150–200, the #131 fix; the pair's whole log is 12.0 MB after the NetworkRoutingProvider logger went to ERROR, §9.142), telemetry.jsonl and _config.json memoised by file stamp (§9.174) — then one atomic 2.3 KB _progress.json write; ceiling watcher: the clock every RUN.gate.ceiling_poll_s 60 s; stall watcher: the log's mtime against RUN.gate.stall_kill_s 1800 s; gate watcher: OFF on every F35 arm (RUN.gate.interval_iterations 0 in the overlays), otherwise a reporter subprocess per 100 iterations retried every 300 s; the live view on 8731 polls every 3 s (0.5 s during the mobsim sweep) from the same memoised readers when a page is open; RunTelemetry inside the JVM writes ~31 × 4.7 MB telemetry_links.json + 31 × 9 KB telemetry_live.json per iteration on the qsim step thread and one 8.5 KB telemetry.jsonl line at iteration end. watch_run.py (§9.176) reads _progress.json, stopwatch.csv and the ITERS listing on demand; nothing writes to the run.

jvm

command
run_matsim.py:2237–2252: java -Xms48g -Xmx48g -XX:+UseParallelGC [-XX:StartFlightRecording=settings=profile,disk=true,dumponexit=true,maxsize=2g,filename=<run>/profile.jfr under RUN.machine.jfr_profile] [-Xlog:gc*:file=<run>/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags under RUN.machine.gc_log, on by default] -cp <201-jar signals stack + .tools/classes> <main> config.xml. No -XX:ParallelGCThreads (JDK default on 24 CPUs: 18), no young-generation sizing (-Xmn / NewRatio default 2 → ~16 GB young of 48), no compressed-oops (48g is above 32 GB, every reference is 8 bytes), no NUMA flag. The collector choice and heap schedule are typed in the launcher, not registry fields (gc_log and jfr_profile are).
heap_rule
RUN.machine.heap_floor_gib 15.6 + RUN.machine.heap_per_fraction_gib 87 × 0.25 = 37.35 GiB; refuse_small_heap refuses less (run_matsim.py:679–689); every F35 arm carries 48g; the registry default RUN.machine.xmx 18g serves the 1 % overlays.
given_vs_peak
pair (gc.log, every 'Pause Full' line parsed): 340 full collections, live after a full collection max 29,243 MB (28.6 GiB), the last at 97,623 s: 41,237 → 20,675 MB; arm 0: 391 fulls, max live 29,262 MB. performance.json's peak_used_mb (43,952 pair / 42,719 arm 0) is MATSim's MemoryObserver 'used RAM' high-water — heap occupancy before a collection under ParallelGC, not live data. Headroom at 48g: ~17.8 GB over the live peak; a full collection reclaims ~20 GB each time. No slope on either arm (the previous report's band medians stand; the pair's fulls at 5.6 h → 21,088 MB live, 9.1 h → 26,623, 12.7 h → 23,470, 27.1 h → 20,675).
gc_cost
pair: full 340 × mean 6.67 s (median 3.0, p90 16.1, max 71.0 s; 50 pauses over 10 s, most in the first 5 h while a browser shared the CPU) = 2,268.5 s + young 7,470 × mean 0.22 s = 1,633 s → 3,902 s = 3.96 % of the 98,591 s wall; arm 0: full 391 × mean 3.7 s (median 2.49, max 47.2) = 1,447.5 s + young 8,586 = 1,307.5 s → 2,755 s = 2.5 %. A full collection every 288 s on the pair and 279 s on arm 0 — one per iteration: each iteration promotes ~20 GB into the old generation (the replanning's new plans and routes, the events pipeline) which the 16 GB young generation cannot hold to the next collection. The position page's 'GC under 1 % of wall' counted the full pauses at their median; the full-file sum is 2.5–4.0 %.
was_the_heap_binding
No on either F35 result (live peak 28.6 GiB under 47.1 GB committed, no OOM, no slope) and no on the running probe (13,528 MB high-water in setup). Yes once: F33's arm 0 (aborted_20260910T222830_300it_25pct) at 14g, OutOfMemoryError in the replanning of it.98 after 6.5 h plus a 13.1 h wedge (§9.165) — since then the heap rule refuses a small heap and the stall kill would cut the wedge. CPU contention lengthens ParallelGC's stop-the-world pauses (the pair's p90 full pause 16 s against arm 0's 6.5 s), so the game on the machine cost GC time as well as mobsim time.
what_would_change_it
a larger young generation (-Xmn 24–28g) or G1/ZGC would cut the once-per-iteration full collection; wall-time only, no model state — 'unmeasured — needs a probe arm'; bounded above by the 2.5–4.0 % GC share. A 40g heap (F32's) would leave ~10 GB over the live peak; 64g does not fit the 63.5 GB host beside the harness.

python

post_run_pipeline_on_the_pair
run.py --close-out at 03:51:02 on 16 Sep (JVM shutdown 03:30:18): close_out() → summarise_run.summarise (_summary.json 03:55:00: ~4 min, of which the events accounting is one ET.iterparse pass over output_events.xml.gz, 1.56 GB gz, summarise_run.py:256–290) → results_store.process(extract=True): report_mode_ridership --trend (modes_trend.txt 04:05:00: ~10 min over 27 readable iterations, the first derivation of each) then --json (modes_final.json 04:05:13: 13 s) → extract_metrics (_metrics.json 04:05:33: ~20 s: trips/legs/output_links tables + one iterparse of the run's own output_transitSchedule, extract_metrics.py:335–375) → fit (_fit.json 04:06:43: ~70 s, calls report_mode_ridership.report once for the goal modes, fit.py:98–180) → mirror to processed/ (04:06:57). Close-out wall 15.9 min = 1 % of the run; the previous report measured the F32 close-out at 9.2 min and arm 0's events pass at 4.35 min.
what_reads_the_events_and_how_many_times
ONE reader in the close-out: summarise_run.events_accounting (departures = arrivals + stuck + unresolved per mode). report_mode_ridership reads an iteration's events.xml.gz only under --truck-stations (:295–380, a regex line scan; the calibration split) — not in the default report, the trend or fit. extract_metrics reads no events (its iterparse is the schedule). So the events stream is decoded once per close-out, not three times as the eighth/ninth reports found; what is still decoded several times are the trips/legs tables: --trend (27 iterations' tables), --json, extract_metrics and fit each run in their own process with their own iteration_reading cache (CACHE_TABLES 6), so the final trips and legs tables (18 + 47 MB gz) are decoded 3–4× at 10–20 s each.
could_one_pass_serve_every_question
for the events: it already does (one pass; the only other consumer is optional). For the tables: one process for the four close-out readers sharing iteration_reading's cache would save 2–6 min per arm (previous report rank 5, ledger not carried — reporting/tooling only). The --trend memo (§9.176: _trend/ beside the run, keyed by the tables' stamps and the reader's source, 40 s → 0.3 s per iteration on a probe) is built and unit-tested but the pair's raw directory holds no _trend/ — its close-out ran before the memo existed, so the memo has not yet been exercised on a result; the running probe's close-out will be the first.
the_trend_memo_decision_9_176
DECISIONS §9.176 (7) records the by-hand cost the memo removes: report_mode_ridership.py --trend re-derived every readable iteration on every call, 'ten minutes of the arm's own CPU paid twenty times' during the pair's watch. The memo is per (run, iteration, truck_stations, reader stamp) under _trend/, --no-cache re-derives; tests/unit/test_trend_memo.py.
observability_readers_while_a_run_is_live
the digest's log read is incremental; run_view memoises by stamp; watch_run.py reads three small files. The 39.8 GB --trend reader of §9.169 is bounded (CACHE_TABLES = 6) and memoised; nothing on the Python side is now a plausible stall, but no artefact records the harness's own CPU or RSS beside the JVM — 'unmeasured — needs a probe arm' (capture_machine_context in progress_digest.py:164 records machine context only at a stall).

build

does_any_producing_script_record_its_wall_time
YES for 12 builders — cities/newcastle/data/_build_timing.json (src/build/build_timing.py, §9.158; outside the hashed manifest set): build_activity_chains 1,180.1 s, build_matsim_network 248.8, build_matsim_plans 141.6, build_matsim_signals 77.6, build_population 26.6, build_charging_dwell_offsets 9.9, build_landuse_parking 4.4, build_level_crossings 4.4, build_gtfs_extras 1.0, build_corridor_layers 0.8, build_mode_targets 0.6, build_zone_attractions 0.2 — total 1,695.98 s (28.3 min), recorded 10–14 Sep 2026. performance.json's build_timing field says 'none recorded: no producing script writes its wall time into a report or the manifest' because collect_performance.py:371 types that string instead of reading the file — the previous report's rank 6 / ledger row 20260914T152907:17 (open) already said so.
what_is_not_timed
the pt2matsim schedule mapping and build_matsim_run_inputs.py (the 30 run-input sets), build_manifest.py, the extract adapters, sample_population.py (the per-run sample), and the per-run setup inside the JVM before iteration 0 (PersonPrepareForSim routing 155,233 persons: 25.3 min on the pair, 00:07:08 → 00:32:23; ~23 min on arm 0; the running probe was still in it 18 min after launch) — 1,868 s of the pair's 98,591 s wall is outside its iterations.
where_the_timing_would_be_written
the same _build_timing.json through build_timing.record() at the end of each untimed builder (ledger :17 names them); the JVM's setup as a setup_s field on _run.json from the launch stamp to the log's 'ITERATION 0 BEGINS' (arm_cost.setup_seconds in the working tree now derives it from the stopwatch when the harness memo is short); and collect_performance.py reading _build_timing.json into performance.json's build_timing instead of the typed string.

warm start

status
unchanged since the previous report: no arm has been warm-started since #192; the cadence that makes it cheap (plans every 25) costs the pair 7 plans-only milestones × ~231 s excess = 27 min and ~8.3 GB (plans 0.90 + experienced 0.28 GB each) over plans-every-100, buying a crash bound of ≤ 25 iterations ≈ 2.4 h + ~25 min of setup routing. Every-50 would halve the dumps (5 fewer ≈ 19 min and ~6 GB) at a 4.8 h bound — ledger row :9's second half, open. Not carried on a warm start: the RNG stream, TravelTimeCalculator link times, the pairing engine's realised times, SCATS state, the taxi fleet's refusal history — a warm-completed arm is a different run (#75, §9.76).

Verdict on the 250-iteration horizon

The 250-iteration horizon of GOAL.md requirement 8 is reachable at the measured pace and has now been executed twice on F35's stack: arm 0 ran 300 in 30.35 h and the routers pair ran exactly 250 in 27.39 h against a 30.0 h ceiling and a 29.3 h quote — 26.87 h inside iterations (175 plain innovating iterations at a 368 s median, 346.5 s when nothing else used the CPU; a 44-iteration tail at 285 s; 4,406 s of milestone excess; 1,352 s for it.0–1) plus 1,868 s of setup and shutdown — with no stall, no gate, no heap event (live peak 28.6 GiB under 48g, no slope) and its harness dead from iteration 34, which cost observability and a 48.8 h misquote but not one machine-second. Where the iteration goes is settled to the second and it is MATSim's, not ours: the mobsim is 233–245 s (64–66 % innovating, 86 % in the tail) executing 2.8 M departures of which 2.3 M are walk legs on the 368 k-link footpath network, at a parallel efficiency the thread probes (10 → 24 threads, 270 → 264 s) and the one JFR profile (24 % of CPU samples for 57 % of wall) say is low and nothing has yet located; replanning is 84–95 s (25 %) of routers on that graph and vanishes at the cutoff; this project's own listeners are 16–20 s (5 %) and the plans dumps 2.3 %; GC is 4.0 % (one full collection per iteration). Nothing measured halves it. The zero-model-cost items are bounded and worth taking before the scoring pair launches: every-50 checkpoints (~19 min and ~6 GB per arm), a young generation sized so the old generation is not collected every iteration (1–3 %, a flag on the next pricing probe), the close-out in one process (2–6 min), the machine kept to itself (~1.1 h of the pair is attributable to a browser and a game in the stopwatch), and detaching by default so the harness outlives the shell. What would halve an arm is one of two unmeasured things and both need a probe arm before they can be priced: the mobsim's serialisation (the barrier, the events pipeline, the transit engine — a JFR thread-state read is ~1.5 h of machine) or the count of walk legs the qsim executes (a modelling choice made on correctness at F34, which opens a family to revisit). At today's pace the five paired arms of #172 are ~27 h each; the scoring pair's own price is the probe now running.

what the comparison says

  • The top rung is still empty across all 55 agent-based rows (7 / 12 / 26 / 10 / 0); this repository, at 2 of 12 inside 10 % on its third result, remains the only project that scores every simulated mode as a target with a band. Nothing added this pass changes that, because nothing was added: five candidate sweeps yielded six exclusions and three unreadable candidates.
  • BEAM CORE - the most complete US platform row - now has its validation named verbatim (Google Maps speeds, HPMS VMT, MTC agency boardings, MTC 2016 shares) and STILL no level fit in print; its only published comparison is route-level ridership CHANGES against pandemic-confounded observations (Van Ness BRT simulated +59 % against an observed 18-79 % band). The field publishes what it validates on far more readily than how well.
  • Sample fraction is mode-dependent, and the field has now said so with a number: BEAM calibrates at 10 %, validates at 30 %, and finds ride-hailing dynamics converge only at 40 %. This project's 25 % is above Mersini & Ziemke's 10 % floor for car flow and on the steep part of BEAM's curve for on-demand modes - which is where taxi (+142.6 %) and ride (-40.8 %) sit.
  • Run cost per resident is not out of line: BEAM CORE's 30 % SFBay weekday takes 'around 12 h' on 50 cores and 512 GB for 7.75 M residents; this project's 25 % Newcastle arm takes 27.39 h for 250 iterations of 622,318 residents on 16 threads and 48 g. What the field does not publish anywhere is a heap at 25 % - and this pass proved a MATSim log is unreadable from here at any scale.
  • The agency world recalibrates mode choice between releases as routine (MWCOG: 'ongoing recalibration of the tour and trip mode choice models' between the November 2025 beta and the April 2026 production release) and reports that its ABM and its four-step model agree 'except for transit ridership and VHD' - the family this project's six STOP modes belong to. Transit is where every agent-based model in the survey is least sure of itself.
  • The first one-field pair reading in the survey is a null: the routers pair moved nothing against arm 0 outside one build's noise. No other row publishes a controlled single-parameter physical-fidelity comparison; the field's physical-fidelity evidence (Barcelona's actuated signals, Berlin's SUMO free speeds, Ziemke & Braun) reports effects, never validation deltas, and this project's first measured delta is zero.
  • The library is now the binding constraint, not the search: three gaps closed by elimination (Brussels/DC fits, Seoul fit, the Kelheim heap), five new dead routes, and the only substantive addition came from two PDFs on hosts that serve files (LBNL, eScholarship). What a pass can add is bounded by readable hosts; the highest-value remaining item (the BEAM CORE calibration report) is one such host away.
  • Motorcycles: Greater Jakarta (Ilahi, Balać & Axhausen 2026) is, on a search summary, the only candidate in the field with a motorcycle mode calibrated against survey shares - and it is unreadable on three hosts. This project's motorbike (-5.5 %) is one of its two modes inside 10 % and has no published comparator yet.

Against arm 0 the routers pair (C.raptor.mode_cost_representation = mode_constant) moved car -0.35 pp, ride +0.17 pp, light rail 772 -> 856 and heavy rail 10,092 -> 10,476 boardings, pt choice-set coverage 17.53 -> 15.78 % - nothing outside one build's noise (section 9.176). Ride's 20.60 % target is still above its 19.11 % coverage, fixed at the seed, on both arms. Convergence: the pair drifts 0.14 pp over it.210-250 against 0.5 pp with a +1.774 pp cutoff snap on car. No arm is running and no approval stands; D7 (what runs next: the roots rebuild, the scoring pair, or the ASC contraction test for bike) is open.

active, in calibration - P4 at HEAD d6f9cdf (16 September 2026, fifty-third session; the routers pair closed out and read, the handoff's by-hand steps codified as tools, a JVM under a dead harness now goes red at the gate). Registry 558 fields, manifest 959 files, 30 assembled run-input sets, 193 run directories per the board. does_best
Every controllable value declared with units, provenance and a sweep or held-fixed rule (558 fields), every living number pinned to its artefact by a check, twelve modes each monitored on its own basis every tenth iteration - and, unique in this survey, a REGISTRY-ENFORCED refusal to fit a constant over a named missing mechanism (C.asc.rail's departure_requires clause). THIS PASS ADDS A SECOND UNIQUENESS, AND IT IS THE HONEST ONE: the project's _fit.json scores mode shares, absolute link counts, trip-length geometry and vehicle occupancy IN ONE ARTEFACT FROM ONE RUN, names its 32 unscorable targets with reasons, and refuses to call a stopped arm a result. Across 53 surveyed projects, the closest published analogues each hold part of that - AToM validates five observation families but calibrates against one; Tallinn optimises three target families at once but reports no per-mode transit rung; the WFRC framework enumerates every validation summary but states outright that not all of them can be met simultaneously. | 2026-09-14: against the three rows added this pass the position sharpens - Cape Town reaches the tap-data rung for ONE operator with ~25 hand-tuned runs; mobiTopp Stuttgart calibrates trip-length distributions and modal split jointly but by eye; Barcelona runs generic actuated signals at 2,035 intersections on full demand for R2 0.81 on counts and nothing else. None scores more than one observation family with a stated band. | 2026-09-14 (tenth pass): the claim is now made against a RESULT with 2 of 12 inside 10 % rather than 0 - and against 55 rows. The two rows added this pass sharpen it from opposite sides: Barcelona-MATSim (2019) validates on counts it never calibrated on and names the excluded demand behind its two misses, which this project's fit module does for its 32 unscorable targets but not yet for its count outliers; Rotterdam-The Hague (2025) removes mode choice from MATSim altogether so that one calibrator owns it, where this project's twelve constants are scored inside the co-evolutionary loop they must survive. | 2026-09-16 (twelfth pass): the claim is now made against a THIRD result and the first one-field pair reading in the survey - a null. The BEAM update this pass sharpens the comparison from the sample side: BEAM calibrates at 10 %, validates at 30 % and states that an on-demand mode needs 40 % before its dynamics settle; this project reads taxi and ride at 25 % and scores them with a band, which no BEAM paper does.

calibration_method
family
coordinate descent over registry-declared sweeps (unchanged, never run to completion) PLUS, NEW AT THIS HEAD AND NEVER RUN, an implemented ASC log-ratio fixed point - src/calibrate/asc_fixed_point.py. Read from the source at HEAD 781cf41, not searched.
what_the_source_says
src/calibrate/calibrate.py:508-533 runs coordinate descent: per round, per free parameter, per grid point across that parameter's registry sweep, a FULL MATSim run -> extract_metrics -> fit -> a weighted scalar objective over declared _fit.json components, keeping a point only if it is feasible against the C4 occupancy and trip-length constraints; the round stops when the improvement falls below delta. The search space is DERIVED FROM THE REGISTRY, not listed in the script: a field is free only if it is source=assumed, carries a scalar sweep and is not held_fixed. The six mode constants are held_fixed under DECISIONS.md 8.5 and are therefore unreachable from the loop by construction - so this project has NO log(target/modelled) ASC loop of any kind. The one constant that is solved, asc_car_passenger, is solved in a separate module (solve_asc_ride.py:101-121) by SECANT INTERPOLATION ON log(ride_per_car) against the observed passenger:driver ratio, and is reported as a CONSTRAINT, not an estimate. The loop refuses to fit more parameters than the objective identifies (four independent numbers) and cannot read a holdout row by construction.
objective_evaluations
coordinate descent: calibrate.py:433 computes the budget as sum(len(grid(p, points_per_param)) for p in free) * max_rounds FULL MATSim runs; at 25% an arm reaching iteration 100 cost 7.66 h wall, so a 3-point 3-parameter 2-round search is ~18 arms and ~140 machine hours. THE LOOP HAS NEVER BEEN RUN TO COMPLETION. The ASC fixed point is far cheaper by design - TWO arms settle the contraction question - and is the only one of the two that has an evaluation count small enough to state in advance. Neither has been executed.
convergence_criterion
round-over-round objective improvement < delta

asc_fixed_point_new_this_pass
src/calibrate/asc_fixed_point.py EXISTS and PROPOSES ONLY; it has NEVER BEEN RUN. It applies delta_i = damping * [ ln(target_i/modelled_i) - ln(target_ref/modelled_ref) ] against car as reference - the same object as the Berry (1994) share inversion and the same expression matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools computes verbatim, with the damping declared on CAL.asc.damping. THREE DESIGN CHOICES ARE UNUSUAL AND WORTH RECORDING: (1) THE TEST IS THE CONTRACTION, NOT THE SHARES - two damped rounds are compared mode by mode, and if |delta| shrinks the residual is a taste that constants will close, while if it does not shrink the deficit is STRUCTURAL and no constant will ever close it. That is a cheap, decisive, published-in-spirit answer to the 'constant or mechanism' question that the agency protocol answers only by ordering. (2) It CANNOT REACH A FROZEN CONSTANT: it reads held_fixed from the registry and refuses, structurally, the way the holdout guard refuses. (3) On heavy rail and light rail the step is marked basis_is_boardings and reported as a PROXY, because the logit inversion is exact only for shares of a common total. ROUND 1 IS PROPOSED OFF THE F31 GATE AND NOT APPLIED: bike -0.5121, bus -0.2301, ferry +0.6713, light rail +0.4143.
read_against_the_field_this_pass
Two published methods now bracket this project's loop and both were read this pass. (1) Chen, Prakash, Lima de Azevedo & Ben-Akiva (2020, TR-C 119:102650) names this project's coordinate descent for what it is: 'myopic heuristics in the sense that they do not consider the fundamental inter-dependencies among choice-models and do not have a systematic way to adjust model parameters' - and their non-myopic alternative calibrates precisely this project's target set at once (activity shares, mode shares, mode-specific OD flows, mode-specific sensor counts). (2) The WFRC/RSG ActivitySim framework publishes New ASC = Old ASC + ln(Target Proportion / Model Proportion) verbatim - the exact expression in asc_fixed_point.py - inside a CYCLIC protocol over model components, and states plainly that 'It is typically the case that not all calibration and validation targets can be achieved simultaneously.' | 2026-09-11 (third bracket): POLARIS's published procedure is the same cyclic ASC-by-purpose update, TIERED by iteration so that 'network state' can 'adapt to this change in demand' before the next tier is touched, with counts and speeds explicitly outside the calibrated set ('can only be minimally calibrated'). MATSim-NYC calibrated NO demand constants at all - its nested logit was estimated on RHTS + TLC/FHV/Citi Bike records and converted analytically - and spent its six SPSA iterations on twelve link-CAPACITY factors instead, which is the opposite allocation to this project's.

MEASURED ONCE NOW: the routers pair (C.raptor.mode_cost_representation = mode_constant, the first of five one-field controls) moved nothing against arm 0 outside one build's noise (car -0.35 pp, light rail +84 boardings, heavy rail +384; section 9.176). warm_start
--warm-start <dead run dir> exists in src/run/run_matsim.py: it resumes from a dead run's newest plans checkpoint, records warm_started_from, and RE-DERIVES RUN.replanning.fraction_to_disable_innovation so the innovation cutoff ITERATION is the parent's (the pinned jar's first + f x (last - first) had moved it 240 -> 260 at N = 100, #192). It is crash recovery, not a bit-identical continuation. Arm 0 of F35 dumps plans every 25 iterations for exactly this reason (the F33 arm that died at 98 had checkpoints at it.0 and it.1 only). This matches the platform's own answer (MATSim issue #834: restart AT the checkpoint iteration from its post-replanning plans); the platform has no finer mechanism, and the interval is the whole trade. No surveyed row states a warm start from a prior calibrated run except as the matsim-scenarios practice of shipping calibrated output plans as input plans. | 2026-09-14: arm 0 ran with warm_started_from: null and dumped plans every 25 iterations (12 checkpoints, 522-898 s each, ~50 min of the arm); it did not need the mechanism. Across the field this pass, Kelheim v3.0's published output is a single 388-iteration run and Rotterdam-The Hague's outer loop restarts MATSim per LOS iteration; no surveyed row checkpoints or warm-starts a calibration arm.

signals_addendum_2026_09_14
Ziemke & Braun 2021 (Procedia CS 184:745-752, doi 10.1016/j.procs.2021.03.093; VSP WP 20-40 read in full): OSM-derived signals and lanes were added to the Open Berlin Scenario and 'one iteration of the co-evolutionary algorithm was run to verify that the automated generation of signal and lane data results in a connected and correct network' - the 'verification' is structural, not against counts or travel times. Default fixed-time plans from German guidelines (90 s cycle, 10 s minimum green, 5 s all-red; extra green by lane count): 'This signal plans do not necessarily model a realistic signal control.' 'As the simulation of traffic signals and lanes in MATSim significantly increases runtime, the automated generation tool provides a possibility to ...' restrict the signalised area; 'only MATSim's Dijkstra implementation works with lanes, which is comparably slow.' Whether signals move a count fit in Berlin remains UNMEASURED in the published record.

    calibration_tooling
    Three named routes, all read this pass: (1) matsim.calibration in matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools - an ASCCalibrator driving an Optuna study, whose update is literally log(z_i) - log(m_i) - (log(z_0) - log(m_0)), i.e. the classic ASC fixed-point loop normalised on a fixed reference mode, with a pluggable learning-rate scheduler and a TerminationCondition dataclass whose check_termination carries "# TODO: not used yet"; (2) Cadyts, a Bayesian count calibration that adjusts NO parameter and instead adds a utility bonus so agents select the plans matching observed counts; (3) opdyts (Flotterod, TR-B 2017), which approximates point equilibria of the mobsim/scoring/replanning loop, with a Berlin mode-constant example. See calibration_methods. | 2026-09-14: the METHOD NOTE behind route (1) is now read in full - Rakow & Nagel, 'Automated calibration of alternative specific constants in agent based transport models', TU Berlin, June 2024, doi 10.14279/depositonce-20593, CC BY 4.0, three pages. Verbatim: 'Perform a simulation run until convergence and collect all relevant trips. Let z_i be the reference mode share for mode i and m_i the simulated mode share. One ASC always has to be fixed (usually to 0); otherwise, the solution is not unique ... asc_i + ln z_i - ln m_i - (ln z_0 - ln m_0) ... Perform more simulation runs while updating asc_i by delta_i for all modes i, except i = 0 after each run. This is done until simulated mode shares are sufficiently close to the reference mode shares.' Proof given for two alternatives under fixed utilities; discussion: 'The proof assumes that utilities remain constant during simulation runs, which is often not the case ... it is recommended to adjust the update step delta_i by a fraction. This fraction can be modified based on the difference between simulated and reference mode shares.' No run count, no scenario, no fit figure, no distance term in the note; the tooling's ASCDistCalibrator adds distance-group constants with the same update. The idea is credited to Gunnar Floetteroed. This is the exact expression in this project's asc_fixed_point.py, and it is cited as the calibration tool by the Rotterdam-The Hague row (Li et al. 2025).
    carried_to
    2026-09-16
    restart_mechanism
    NO checkpoint/resume exists in the platform. The developer answer (Marcel Rieser, matsim-code-examples issue #834, 12 Dec 2022, read via api.github.com this pass): 'The plans in "it200/200.plans.xml.gz" are the plans after replanning, but before mobsim, in iteration 200. So you can use those to resume at iteration 200 (it should generate the same events file like the first run), and then continue with iteration 201.' and 'If you use the plans file of iteration 200, start the new run also with iteration 200.' ... 'The first iteration of a run never does replanning.' So a resume is a plans-file restart AT the checkpoint iteration, and only where a plans dump exists (writePlansInterval); everything since the last dump is lost. Memory rule of thumb from the same repository's issue #189: 'typically... around 100KB per agent. That is 1 GB per 10k agents' (mrieser, 2019-08-20); a ~1M-agent, 250k-link scenario needed 60-90 GB actual (mrieser); JVM total is ~25% above the reported heap (josiekre).

What the field does NOT publish is a flow TOLERANCE. The FHWA validation manual chapter 3 states there are no criteria guidelines for trip-distribution checks, and AToM - the leading open Australian activity- and agent-based model, and the source of several of this project's own behavioural coefficients - validates work travel only as a MODE SHARE of work trips, against a stated plus-or-minus one per cent error threshold on the 2016 Census Method of Travel to Work: driving 74.8% simulated against 73.4% VISTA and 75.2% census; public transport 21.5 / 21.4 / 19.3; walking 2.1 / 2.5 / 3.7; cycling 1.6 / 2.7 / 1.7. Destination distributions are shown only VISUALLY, at SA3 level, with no quantitative flow metric reported, and non-work trips are far looser (walking 15.4% simulated against 23.1% in VISTA). The transferable benchmark for a workplace-location build is therefore: work-trip mode share inside about one percentage point of the census table, plus a visual destination check - not an origin-destination pair tolerance, which no Australian activity-based model publishes.https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.120712026-09-08

Class IN unchanged.counts +14.3 % mean / GEH unread on the pair: route choice is not what the board is short of; the new delay measure is the first per-link congestion reading the project can compare with a map app.Route choice is estimated on GPS-observed routes with path-size logit corrections for overlapping paths, and the observed share taking the shortest path is small: over 25,157 trips by 143 subjects tracked for 8-13 weeks in Minneapolis-St Paul, 34% of all trips exactly matched the shortest-travel-time path and 40% matched within a 10% tolerance, while for commute trips alone the figures were 13.5% and 21.7%; no subject followed a shortest-DISTANCE path unless it coincided with the shortest-time one. Class IN unchanged.car +1.774 pp and walk -1.344 pp at the cutoff on the pair (arm 0 +1.683 / -1.245): the cutoff moves modes on every result; the MSA member is the D7 arm.The distinction that governs convergence: while innovation is switched on - new routes, new times - the result is NOT truly stationary; if innovation is switched off the process is stationary but limited to the plans each agent holds at that moment. The plan set is the agent's choice set, and MATSim's recommended control is fractionOfIterationsToDisableInnovation rather than a per-strategy disable iteration. ADDED 8 September 2026: what the loop is converging TO is stated by MATSim's own equilibrium work - an approximate minimisation of an equilibrium gap that measures, per agent, how much it could improve by changing its plan while all others keep theirs; 'the gap is always non-negative and zero at a (possibly non-existing) Nash equilibrium'. Class PARTIAL unchanged.every deviation; the loop has no finished evaluation.Calibrating a microsimulation is a black-box, stochastic, expensive simulation-based optimisation problem, and the published methods separate by how many simulation evaluations they can afford. SPSA (simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation) is the field's workhorse because it costs only two simulation evaluations per gradient estimate whatever the dimension, and W-SPSA extends it with a weight matrix; but it is built for asymptotic guarantees rather than early termination, and under a small budget it barely moves - on a Salt Lake City origin-destination calibration of order thirty thousand dimensions SPSA took the vehicle-count nRMSE from 120% to 117% over fifteen simulation iterations, while a metamodel method reached 32%. Evolutionary strategies (CMA-ES, xNES) and finite-difference gradient approximation (FDSA, SPSA) are what the MATSim/eqasim calibration framework boptx implements. The cross-entropy method is a Monte-Carlo importance-sampling search and is the most expensive family: one published SUMO calibration of a three-intersection model spent 98,304 simulation evaluations. Bayesian optimisation over a surrogate is the current answer for a small budget (see the surrogate row). The field states its own constraint plainly: computational budgets in the literature are 'one to two orders of magnitude lower than the problem dimension', and general-purpose algorithms 'are designed for asymptotic performance guarantees and are not designed to be terminated with such few function evaluations'.https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.113922026-09-08

The counting rule underneath is what binds a mode-share calibration: K shares that sum to one contain K-1 independent numbers, so scoring twelve modelled modes against a five-mode survey does not supply twelve independent targets. The only way to buy identifiability for more parameters is to add targets of a DIFFERENT kind - link counts, boardings, trip-length and duration distributions - not more shares of the same total. In dynamic OD calibration, 'the first formulation estimates the whole set of time-dependent OD matrices SIMULTANEOUSLY for the entire time period in one calibration round. The second formulation estimates and calibrates OD matrices SEQUENTIALLY one at a time for each time frame. Most optimization-based studies have used the simultaneous approach, since the available sequential methods may lose accuracy due to giving up some information in the transition between time frames' - while the simultaneous form 'is incapable of handling a stream of data for real-time or online demand calibration'. The same paper states the bind that makes the choice matter at all: 'this optimization problem is underdetermined for large-scale networks since the number of roads with traffic measurement is usually several orders of magnitude smaller than the number of all roads in the network', and it names the standard architecture as BI-LEVEL - an upper-level discrepancy minimisation over an inner assignment that must be re-solved at every candidate, where 'performing several DTAs for each optimization task demand considerable computational resources'. In DTA practice the sequential form is supply first and then demand with the supply held fixed; the reported weakness of decomposing is that the stages need not be internally consistent, because each stage's assumed input is not the other stage's output.https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.173152026-09-09

The leading open MATSim calibrator, matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools, computes the raw step verbatim as 'math.log(z_i) - math.log(m_i) - (math.log(z_0) - math.log(m_0))' and applies it under a SCHEDULE whose default is 'linear_scheduler(start=0.6, end=1, interval=3)' - the early rounds take 0.6 of the raw step and the fraction relaxes to the full step over three intervals, i.e. cautious while the shares are far from target and undamped once they are near. The agency practice in the ActivitySim world applies a FLAT dampener instead of a schedule. Neither publishes a convergence proof, and the same library's 'TerminationCondition.check_termination' still carries '# TODO: not used yet' - so the field's standard answer ships a damping default and no working stopping rule at all. The undamped step (1.0) is the boundary case: it is what a fixed point converges to when it converges, and what overshoots when the shares are far out.https://github.com/matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools/blob/master/matsim/calibration/utils.py2026-09-09

Jakob and Blume set it out: with a weighted sum, 'by varying the weights, any point of a convex Pareto front can be obtained... On the other hand, it is possible that parts of the Pareto front cannot be found in case of a non-convex problem... the part between points A and B of the Pareto front cannot be obtained for any weights. This is a serious drawback.' The counterweight is cost: 'the computational effort to determine all or at least most of the Pareto front increases significantly with the number of conflicting objectives', and the paper's framing is that the real-world question arises 'where either more than four objectives have to be considered, or the same type of task is repeated again and again with only minor modifications'. So beyond about four conflicting targets a full Pareto treatment is expensive and scalarisation is the practical route - while the scalarisation chosen decides which compromises are reachable at all. A weighted sum of squared deviations across targets is the standard form in simulation-based transport calibration.https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.026972026-09-09

The selection protocol before the cutoff 'resembles a MNL choice model', P(i|C) = exp(mu S_i)/sum exp(mu S_j) with mu = brainExpBeta, and the chapter notes that BestPlanSelector is the same selector with an infinite mu. So the pre-cutoff share is a logit-dispersed mixture over each agent's remembered plans and the post-cutoff share is the same population collapsed toward its arg-max: switching innovation off changes the estimator, not only the amount of search. Assignment theory says the same thing from the other side - a low dispersion parameter concentrates flow on the perceived-best alternative and the pattern approaches deterministic user equilibrium, which is the classic 'unrealistic route concentration' that stochastic user equilibrium was introduced to cure. The efficiency loss of that concentration is bounded and modest on real networks - a data-driven estimate for Eastern Massachusetts puts the price of anarchy near 1.30, and other empirical work finds it close to 1 in both light and heavy traffic - so an equilibrium being reached is no guarantee that it resembles the observed day, which is itself a non-equilibrium average.https://matsim.org/docs/userguide/terminology.html2026-09-10

Class PARTIAL unchanged.car +9.0 rising after it.100 on both results, bike +197.8, taxi +142.6 through selection: the SelectRandom and MSA controls are the two arms that test it; the MSA one is next (D7).Habit is one of the two strongest predictors of the mode a person uses, and it is a MEASURED effect, not a residual. Three meta-analyses put the pooled correlation between a habit measure and the travel mode used at r+ = 0.50 (Gardner & Abraham 2008), r+ = 0.42 (Lanzini & Khan 2017, 58 primary studies) and r = 0.47 (Hoffmann et al. 2017), against an averaged pooled car-use-intention correlation of r+ = 0.83 in Lanzini & Khan; the review of reviews that collects them (Javaid, Creutzig & Bren d'Amour 2020) notes the differences between the meta-analyses exceed their confidence intervals. In discrete-choice terms inertia is the tendency to stick with the past choice even when another alternative becomes more appealing: Cherchi & Manca (2011, Transportation 38:679-695) test eight specifications on an RP/SP dataset with a mixed logit and find a significant, mode-specific inertia that weakens with learning across the SP experiments; Cantillo, Ortuzar & Williams (2007, Transportation Science) model it as a randomly distributed inertia THRESHOLD with serial correlation. The route-choice literature measures the same thing as an INDIFFERENCE BAND: travellers do not switch unless the saving exceeds a threshold (Mahmassani & Liu 1999), and Zhu & Levinson (2016, Transportation) estimate lognormal bands on 78 GPS subjects around the Minneapolis I-35W bridge replacement, which explains why the new bridge attracted less traffic than its time saving predicted. Satisficing (Simon 1957) is the general form - search stops at a satisfactory alternative - and boundedly rational user equilibrium (Di & Liu 2016 review) is the assignment that follows from it. The magnitudes the field reports are correlations and thresholds, not a utility constant; a simulator represents habit either as a state-dependent term (past mode in the utility), as a switching threshold, or - as MATSim does - as a selection rule over remembered plans.https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/aba0322026-09-14

Class PARTIAL unchanged.Little on the current board; the Zhu & Levinson band (half of routes within 30 s of fastest, 90 % within 5 min) is the check a routing randomness of 3.0 has never been read against.Reliability enters route choice as a second attribute beside mean time, and the field's summary statistic is the RELIABILITY RATIO - the value of a unit of standard deviation over the value of a unit of mean travel time. Carrion & Levinson (2012, TR-A 46(4):720-741) review and meta-analyse the estimates and attribute their spread to measurement (which dispersion measure, SP versus RP, self-reported versus GPS times). The same authors' Minneapolis before-and-after study of the I-35W bridge (39 subjects with complete data, 78 GPS observations) shows how far the ratio moves with measurement alone: 1.30 (mean/SD) and 1.60 (median/SD) on SELF-REPORTED times against 0.42 and 0.77 on GPS-MEASURED times, and 0.83 / 0.39 on the mean-to-90th-percentile measure - a ratio above 1 with perceived times and below 1 with measured ones. Route SWITCHING is boundedly rational: travellers keep their usual route until the saving exceeds an indifference band (Mahmassani & Liu 1999; Zhu & Levinson 2016 estimate lognormal bands on the same 78-subject GPS panel and use them to explain why the replaced bridge attracted less traffic than its time saving implied). For a simulator this means (a) a reliability term in route cost needs a measured day-to-day time variance per link, which a single-day equilibrium simulation does not produce, and (b) the switching rate of the route-choice strategy is itself a behavioural parameter.https://findingspress.org/article/8330-uncovering-the-influence-of-commuters-perception-on-the-reliability-ratio2026-09-14

In-flight work seen in the tree

The tree at the commit read carried this session's uncommitted work, all of it described here and none of it built on by the lanes: (1) D6 taken - run.py detaches by default on Windows, --foreground opts out, the scheduled child is re-invoked with --foreground; README updated; (2) the pricer's setup_seconds() reads the JVM's own stopwatch when the harness memo is short (the 48.8 h misquote), with three tests; (3) preflight(dry_run=True) no longer refuses a dry run under a running arm; (4) the scoring-pair overlay f35_scoring_msa_25pct (one field, plans every 50, ceiling from the probe); (5) #213 - the launcher writes _residents.csv.gz at subsample, the readers prefer it, the store mirrors it, the two F35 results backfilled with a note, three tests; (6) lane.json records D6 and D7; (7) the metrics collector splits its PR query per PR with a retry on GitHub's 5xx. The 25 % pricing probe was running during the pass and the scoring pair launches on its price.

Since the last report, and the report process itself

Findings. Of the eleventh report's 70 embedded findings, the code lane re-checked every one at HEAD: 8 closed, 8 changed, 54 still open. The document lane closed 13 of the previous pass's 30 contradictions and found 13 new (25 stand). Two defects are new this pass and both were fixed in the same tree before the report was written (the pricer's orphan setup; the run's own residents map, #213). Survey rows. 55 projects and 12 platforms carried; 1 updated (BEAM CORE, its validation data named verbatim and a 40 % sample floor for ride-hail), 0 added, 6 excluded, 3 gaps closed and 2 added; the top rung stays empty across the field. Factor statuses. 101 rows (5 new: immobility, station access mode, walk-access distance, travel-time validation, mobile-phone OD): IN 47 / PARTIAL 39 / INERT 3 / ASC 1 / OUT 11 - no class changed since the eleventh report, because no registry value and no scoring Java moved between b8f89ff and d6f9cdf; the proofs of F5 and E25 moved from 'built, unrun' to 'run, a null' (the routers pair). Recommendations. Of the eleventh report's 20: 10 taken within a day (six in the PR that lodged it), 10 open at HEAD; this pass takes three more in its own tree (#20 the cadence - this report follows one reading; #9 plans every 50 on the scoring overlay; #11 the run's own residents) and launches the scoring pair the tenth and eleventh both put after the routers pair. The scoreboard did not move: the routers pair (the first recommended control ever executed) read 2 of 12 inside and 6 past the bar, every share within 0.35 pp of arm 0 - a null inside one build's noise.

verdict

followed
Yes, and fast: 197 recommendations over eleven reports, 151 taken (16 partial), 2 overtaken, 1 repeated-only, 43 open - 77 %. Report #11's 20: 10 taken within a day (six in the same PR that lodged it), 10 open. What is taken is what a session can do alone in hours - readers, launchers, gates, document rules, hidden constants.
moved_the_scoreboard
No. The goal count went 0 -> 2 of 12 between reports #7 and #10 on the footpath rebuild and the engines' routing (F34/F35) - neither a recommendation. The first recommended model-side control ever executed, the routers pair (rec 3 of #11, and of #8, #9, #10 before it), ran 27.39 h and moved nothing outside one build's noise (§9.176). Gates fired since the first report: 6 of the series' 25, none since 8 Sep; arms to horizon: 3. Twelve reports have not moved a single mode across the 10 % line.
what_keeps_not_being_taken
The same four things, each needing something other than a code change: the TfNSW request (six consecutive reports, drafted twice, searched once, never sent - the user's D2), the replication band (seven reports; no second-seed arm since 21 Aug), a second reviewer (three reports; 0 reviews on 77 PRs; the status checks are now required, the reviewer is not), and any rebuild of the demand at its roots (the population-synthesis lane of #4, 0 of 7; the roots rebuild of #10 and #11). The open set is now the set of things that cost an approval, an external party or a family boundary.
cadence
The rule since 11 Sep is once per reading. This is the first pass that follows its reading (the pair's horizon, 16 Sep) with nothing in between and reads a RESULT rather than an unfinished arm - it meets the rule's letter and purpose. Before it: eleven reports over 16 readings in 13 days, four on 7 Sep, two on 14 Sep straddling one arm. The cost of that cadence shows in the re-reporting (163 findings chained across two or more consecutive reports through #10, 15 more from #10 to #11) and in the ledger: the repeats are now the majority of what a report recommends.

Appendix

Reproduce: python src/run/session_gate.py; the three collectors under .claude/skills/project-report/scripts/ into a scratch directory; the six lane prompts are in the skill's Phases 2-7; render_report.py <scratch> docs/reports/<stamp>_project_report.html. Search rounds: field 12 rounds / 37 calls; factors 6 rounds / 20 calls. Sources: every row of the reference library carries its URLs and last_verified date; the report-data block at the end of this file holds the lanes' JSON for the next pass's diff. Rubric: correctness (no defect = 4+, a 5 needs no open risk), maintainability (functions under 150 lines and complexity 15, no duplicate helper), efficiency (no repeated parse of a growing file, no row-wise pandas over the population), testability (the module imported by a unit test on the fixture city), constraint compliance (the hard constraints of .claude/CLAUDE.md, read against the ledger of check_hardcoding.py).
